title: Air India Combined Loss More Than Doubles to ₹22,238 Crore in FY26
excerpt: Tata Group-owned Air India and Air India Express posted a record combined net loss as revenue slipped 9%, with chairman N. Chandrasekaran framing the turnaround as a five-to-ten-year journey.
body:
• Air India and Air India Express posted a combined net loss of ₹22,238 crore (about $2.6 billion) in FY26, more than double the ₹10,859 crore loss a year earlier.
  • Combined revenue fell nearly 9% to ₹71,870 crore even as total expenses rose to ₹93,733 crore, with aircraft repair and maintenance costs climbing to ₹14,976 crore.
  • Chairman N. Chandrasekaran told shareholders the rebuild is a five-to-ten-year journey: "every great airline in history was built over decades, not quarters."
  • Bloomberg reported Tata Group and Singapore Airlines are in talks to inject fresh capital, though the sum under discussion may not fully cover the airline's needs.

Tata Group-owned Air India and its budget arm Air India Express reported a record combined net loss of ₹22,238 crore (about $2.6 billion) in the fiscal year ended March 2026 — more than double the ₹10,859 crore loss recorded a year earlier — underscoring how steep the path back to profitability remains four years after privatisation.

The figures, drawn from the airlines' annual reports, show combined revenue fell nearly 9 per cent to ₹71,870 crore even as the carriers continued to spend heavily on the rebuild. According to fresh analysis this week citing Moneycontrol, PTI and regulatory filings, consolidated total expenses rose to ₹93,733.31 crore in 2025-26 from ₹89,317.12 crore the previous fiscal.

The numbers behind the loss

Air India, the full-service carrier, posted revenue of ₹51,452 crore and a net loss of ₹15,368 crore. Air India Express, the low-cost subsidiary, reported revenue of ₹19,088 crore alongside a net loss of ₹6,767 crore. Consolidated total income slipped from ₹78,635.61 crore to ₹71,869.94 crore.

Costs stayed stubbornly high. Aircraft repair and maintenance climbed to ₹14,976.45 crore from ₹13,901.82 crore a year earlier, reflecting an ageing fleet undergoing renewal and prolonged supply-chain disruptions for components. Fuel expenses declined to ₹26,871.80 crore from ₹29,023.37 crore, offering some relief.

The ownership picture: Tata Sons holds 73.82 per cent of Air India, Singapore Airlines 25.1 per cent, and employees own 1.08 per cent through a share benefit scheme created at the 2022 privatisation.

A five-to-ten-year journey

In his message to shareholders, Air India chairman N. Chandrasekaran framed the transformation as a long-horizon undertaking rather than a turnaround measurable in quarters.

"Every great airline in history was built over decades, not quarters."

— N. Chandrasekaran, Chairman, Air India

Chandrasekaran cited the condition in which the airline was acquired from the government, prolonged supply chain disruptions affecting aircraft components, the need to modernise legacy systems and processes, fleet renewal, cultural change and building a large pool of skilled technical and aviation professionals. His remarks signal that the Tata Group's multi-billion-dollar commitment will need to extend well beyond initial timelines.

Headwinds: crash, airspace, rising costs

The fiscal year was brutal for the carrier. The fatal AI171 accident in June 2025 reversed earlier recovery momentum, and route disruptions — including the Pakistan airspace closure — added costs and lengthened flight times on key international sectors. According to reporting on the results, the eventual loss was far worse than the $1.6 billion figure the airline had privately estimated just months earlier.

The bailout question

The scale of the losses has pushed Air India back to its owners for money, Bloomberg reported. Tata Group and Singapore Airlines are both in discussions to pump in fresh funds — though the amount under consideration may not be enough to fully cover what the airline needs, which could force the carrier to seek additional sources of financing.

Singapore Airlines, which entered Air India as a minority shareholder after merging its Indian affiliate Vistara with the carrier in 2024, has seen its own earnings dragged down by Air India's performance. Earlier this month, Air India appointed UK-based aircraft marketing and asset management firm Skytech-AIC to oversee the sale of six Airbus A319 aircraft — a small but telling step in the fleet-renewal effort.

What it means for travellers

For the diaspora — the airline's lifeblood on India–Gulf, India–UK and India–North America routes — a financially strained Air India raises competing possibilities: fare pressure as the carrier tries to cover costs, and continued network expansion funded by fresh capital. The carrier remains the largest international operator out of India, and its financial health directly affects the reliability of the air links connecting millions of overseas Indians to home.

What's next

Watch the capital-raise talks between Tata and Singapore Airlines — the size and structure of any fresh infusion will set the terms of the next phase of the turnaround. The fleet renewal programme, progress on stabilising revenue in FY27 and whether the carrier can bring maintenance and operating costs under control will determine whether Chandrasekaran's decade-long timeline holds. For now, the ₹22,238-crore loss stands as the costliest year yet of the Tata era.
